mcqs.question: Two bidders submit a valid winning bid within milliseconds of each other. What guarantees only one of them actually wins that round?
options: Serializing access to the current-high-bid value — via a row lock or an atomic compare-and-swap with a version check — so only one write can succeed
The bidding system processes bids in the order the bidders' browsers were opened
Both bids are accepted and the higher one is picked at the very end of the auction
Whichever bidder has bid more times in the past automatically wins ties
mcqs.explanation: The current high bid is a single mutable value under contention, so serialized access (a lock or atomic compare-and-swap) is what makes one write win deterministically. Browser open order and bid history aren't part of the logic, and accepting both bids would corrupt the auction's state.

mcqs.question: When a ProxyBid reacts to a new competing bid, why does it counter-bid min(needed, maxAmount) instead of jumping straight to the stored maximum?
options: Bidding the maximum immediately would be technically invalid in most auction systems
It only ever needs to bid the smallest amount required to retake the lead, keeping the bidder's true ceiling hidden from competitors
The maximum amount is only used for display purposes, never for actual bidding
It avoids having to store the maximum amount in the database at all
mcqs.explanation: Bidding just enough to lead — capped at the max — is exactly what keeps the true ceiling private, which is the point of proxy bidding. Bidding the max outright is legal, just strategically pointless; the max is genuinely used (as the cap), and it still needs to be stored.

mcqs.question: What's the main trade-off of an anti-snipe extension window compared to a hard close time?
options: It makes proxy bidding technically impossible to implement
It removes the need for a minimum bid increment
It reflects true willingness to pay better, at the cost of the end time no longer being fully predictable in advance
It eliminates the need to lock the auction row when placing a bid
mcqs.explanation: The real trade is fairness against sniping versus a fixed, predictable end time — anti-snipe wins on fairness but the close time can shift. It has no bearing on proxy bidding, minimum increments, or row locking during bid placement.

mcqs.question: Why is an Observer-based outbid notification preferable to having each bidder's client poll for status?
options: Polling every few seconds is simpler to implement and delivers notifications just as instantly as an event-driven approach
Observers eliminate the need to ever track who the currently highest bidder is
Polling is required by most payment providers before a bid can be confirmed
An event fires exactly once, right when a bidder is outbid, reaching only the affected bidders — no wasted polling requests, and far less notification lag
mcqs.explanation: Event-driven notification fires precisely when needed to exactly the right bidders, unlike polling which wastes requests and still lags. There's no such platform requirement for polling, and the highest bidder still needs to be tracked regardless of notification method.
